data.commands#What each command does: create --fs exfat formats the volume through the container itself (go-filesystems/exfat FormatImage). No decrypted copy is ever written to disk. serve unlocks the container and serves its exFAT over SMB (2.1 to 3.1.1, signed) using go-filesystems/smb v0.13.0. serve --mount mounts the share in the file manager (Finder, GNOME Files, Explorer) with no password dialog, through go-fileshare/automount: the password goes to the operating system’s mount service as a value. At stop it unmounts first, so the client flushes through the server, then commits and closes the container. --credentials-out is no longer required when --mount is given. --credentials-out writes the URL, user and password to a file (mode 0600, created only if absent, removed at exit), for another client. One of --mount and --credentials-out is required. Writes are committed to the container every --sync (default 5 s) and when the server stops.
data.limit#A limit: A copy of a file written through the share is one transaction per journal budget, not one per file (DESIGN section 19, I12). A crash in the middle of a large copy can leave the exFAT metadata of that copy half-written, as on a disk.
data.measured#Measured, and where: Measured on macOS 27 only (2026-11-16): --mount lands in /Volumes/theca over SMB 3.1.1 signed with AES-128-GMAC, a file written through it survives a stop and a remount, and verify passes. Linux (GNOME Files, through gvfs) and Windows (Explorer, a drive letter through MSFT_SmbMapping) use the same command; neither has been measured with theca yet.
data.security#Security: Loopback only. The data is decrypted, and the SMB server still accepts a replayed frame (go-filesystems/smb#53) and an unsigned request on a session that requires signing (go-filesystems/smb#54). serve therefore listens on a loopback address only, while those two issues are open. One random account per run, never printed or passed as an argument.
data.serve#Serving the files inside:
Since v0.2.0, Theca can hold an exFAT filesystem and serve it over SMB, so a container is used like a disk without ever writing a decrypted copy. This page is written from the README at tag v0.2.0 (section “Serving the files inside”) and its CHANGELOG; where it differs from the repository, the repository wins.
theca create vault.theca --size 4G --fs exfat # a container holding an exFAT filesystem theca serve vault.theca --mount # appears in the Finder; Ctrl-C unmounts and stops # serving smb://127.0.0.1:58738/theca; Ctrl-C to stop # mounted at /Volumes/theca theca serve vault.theca --credentials-out creds.json # or: hand the account to another client

data.cli#Command line:
go install github.com/go-theca/theca/cmd/theca@latest theca create vault.theca --size 1G # asks the password twice, prints the recovery code once theca info vault.theca # unlock and describe theca verify vault.theca # authenticate every sector and tree node theca import vault.theca --password-file pw --offset 0 < disk.img theca export vault.theca --password-file pw > disk.img theca enroll-key vault.theca --recovery-file rc # pair the key with the password and the recovery code theca info vault.theca --fido2 # password + key theca info vault.theca --recovery-file rc --fido2 # recovery code + key Secrets never go in arguments or environment variables. The password is read from the terminal with echo off, or from --password-file. The recovery code is read from --recovery-file. Both files must be regular files that only their owner can read (mode 0600 or stricter); anything else is refused. create prints the recovery code once, on standard output. If you redirect it to a file, that file gets your umask (often 0644): restrict it, or better, write the code down on paper. import reads its data from standard input, so it needs --password-file or --recovery-file. It is not one atomic transaction: on an error, the bytes written before the error are kept. enroll-key makes one discoverable credential on the key (relying party theca, credProtect 3, hmac-secret) and pairs it with the password, and with the recovery code too when --recovery-file names it. The key is touched twice: to register, then to confirm. --fido2 adds the attached key to an unlock. A key without a fingerprint asks for its PIN, read from --pin-file (mode 0600 or stricter) or from the terminal, never from an argument. theca create --fs exfat and theca serve (with --mount) are described in Serving and mounting.
Not in this version: FIDO2 on Linux and Windows, the TPM counter, and slot management on the command line (go-theca/theca#5).
data.factors#Factors:
A container is opened by one of three factors:
a password, stretched with Argon2id; a recovery code, printed once by create and never stored; a FIDO2 security key, which is never a factor alone: it always pairs with the password or with the recovery code. The policy is chosen at creation. --policy any (the default) lets the password alone, or the recovery code alone, open the container. --policy 2of3 needs two of the three: password and recovery code from the start, and a FIDO2 key (enroll-key) then pairs with each.
data.performance#Performance:
Theca is measured against C references on one core with go-scikit/refbench: libsodium for XChaCha20 and Argon2id, OpenSSL for AES-256-CTR and HMAC-SHA-256. The procedure and the cases are in bench/README.md. Ratio is Go time divided by reference time; below 1 is faster. Both runs are on commit 6d515c5 with go1.27.4, libsodium 1.0.22 and OpenSSL 4.0.2, from 2026-11-15. Medians in ns/call; the full tables, with quartiles and allocation counts, are docs/perf-table.md and docs/perf-zen4-table.md.
case Apple M4 Max (Go / ref, ratio) AMD Zen 4 (Go / ref, ratio) Sector/XChaCha20 2286 / 4143, 0.55 faster 4016 / 9195, 0.44 faster (see caveat) Sector/AES-256-CTR 459.4 / 308.9, 1.49 slower 432.7 / 357.1, 1.21 slower Sector/Tag (HMAC-SHA-256) 1493 / 1428, 1.05 slower 1691 / 1736, 0.97 faster Sector/Seal 4290 / 5935, 0.72 faster 6140 / 11330, 0.54 faster Sector/Open 4296 / 5992, 0.72 faster 6154 / 11380, 0.54 faster Argon2id t3-m64MiB-p1 9.424e+07 / 6.306e+07, 1.49 slower 6.616e+07 / 2.662e+08, 0.25 faster (see caveat) The Apple M4 Max run was at a 1-minute load of 7.22 to 7.59 (gate 8.00); the Zen 4 machine is an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X pinned to one CPU, at a load of 0.16 to 0.35. Both runs are marked valid. A gap in a row includes Theca’s own per-sector setup cost, which is a cost of the design and not of the language.
Open slower rows, each tracked as an issue:
#8: Sector/AES-256-CTR is slower than OpenSSL. #9: Sector/Tag (HMAC-SHA-256) is slower than OpenSSL. #10: Argon2id is slower than libsodium on arm64 (no NEON kernel in x/crypto/argon2). Caveat on the Zen 4 libsodium rows. On that machine libsodium’s XChaCha20 and Argon2id run far below their usual AVX2 speed (about 440 MB/s, and 4 times slower than Go’s Argon2id). The registry’s libsodium may be built without its SIMD code. Until a control with another libsodium build settles this, the “faster” verdicts in those two rows are not claims.
Source: https://github.com/go-theca/theca.
data.security#Security notes:
The threat model is DESIGN section 1. The places where the code differs from, or fixes the details of, the design are in its section 19, the implementation log; the FIDO2 design and its trade-offs are in HARDWARE-KEYS.md section 9, “H2 revised”.
Known limits, as the repository states them:
No rollback counter in the command line yet. Every command that opens a container says whether it is protected against rollback; in this version it never is, so an older copy of a container would be accepted. FIDO2 works on macOS only for now (through go-macos/fido). It was tested on a YubiKey 5, firmware 5.7.4. A reader of the FIDO2 salt can test password guesses. The salt that a key is asked for is derived from the partner factor, so for whoever reads it (a forged authenticator, a leaked log) it is a password verifier, at Argon2id cost per guess. The salts are wiped after each call and never logged (DESIGN section 19, I21). Revoked factors: older copies of a container still open with a factor that was removed (DESIGN section 19, I15). Tree area: a container at rest is indistinguishable from random except the Merkle tree area, which shows how sparse the container is (DESIGN section 19, I11).
data.theca#theca:
Theca is an encrypted container format in pure Go, with a library and a command line. The library gives an io.ReaderAt and io.WriterAt over the logical volume, and the command line creates, inspects, verifies, imports and exports containers. Since v0.2.0 it also serves the files inside over SMB and mounts them: see Serving and mounting.
Release: v0.2.0 (tag v0.2.0 of go-theca/theca; install with go install github.com/go-theca/theca/cmd/theca@v0.2.0). What changed is in the CHANGELOG at v0.2.0. The format may still change before v1. This page is written from that tag; where it differs from the repository, the repository wins. Its links to the repository’s design documents still point at tag v0.1.0, and the performance tables below were measured on the v0.1.0 commit.
data.what#What it is:
From the README:
authenticated sectors: XChaCha20 xor AES-256-CTR, with HMAC-SHA-256; a Merkle tree over the sector tags, and a write-ahead journal; no magic bytes; keyslots opened by a password (Argon2id), a recovery code, or both; an optional hardware rollback counter. The design, its threat model, the sources it rests on and the decisions taken are in docs/DESIGN.md; section 0 is a one-table summary.
